t: Automatic Taxonomy Builder: a plain-language overview
title: Automatic Taxonomy Builder: a plain-language overview
description: Overview: what the Automatic Taxonomy Builder does and why archives need it. An automatic taxonomy builder looks at a pile of records and grows a family tree of subjects from them. It notices which topics belong together, groups them, then groups the groups — from broad subjects like 'science' down to narrow ones like 'amateur telescope making'. The result is a browsable hierarchy nobody had to draw by hand.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Automatic Taxonomy Builder works
title: How the Automatic Taxonomy Builder works
description: Overview: what the Automatic Taxonomy Builder does and why archives need it. Real builders combine bottom-up and top-down methods: agglomerative clustering merges similar documents using TF-IDF or embedding similarity, while hypernym patterns ('X is a kind of Y', 'Y such as X') mined from text suggest parent-child links. Term co-occurrence builds the first draft of the tree, and label selection picks the most representative term per node. The tree is pruned by minimum cluster size and validated by checking that siblings are genuinely similar and parents genuinely broader.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.

t: How the Automatic Taxonomy Builder works: the deep tour
title: How the Automatic Taxonomy Builder works: the deep tour
description: Overview: what the Automatic Taxonomy Builder does and why archives need it. Real builders combine bottom-up and top-down methods: agglomerative clustering merges similar documents using TF-IDF or embedding similarity, while hypernym patterns ('X is a kind of Y', 'Y such as X') mined from text suggest parent-child links. Term co-occurrence builds the first draft of the tree, and label selection picks the most representative term per node. The tree is pruned by minimum cluster size and validated by checking that siblings are genuinely similar and parents genuinely broader. Advanced builders use embedding-based clustering with dimensionality reduction, let a human curator pin or rename nodes without breaking the algorithm's ability to re-run, and measure tree quality with hierarchy-aware metrics like tree-edit distance against expert taxonomies. The limits are genuinely ambiguous subjects that belong in two places — handled with polyhierarchy (multiple parents) rather than forced single placement — and sparse collections where there is not enough text to cluster reliably, which the builder reports instead of inventing structure.
provenance: Public methods compiled from standard information-extraction and knowledge-organization practice. Assembled for the JAH Databases archive.
